2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable to single-timepoint qualitative interviews (note: initial invitation refusal count is unreported, and >70% of the 19 interviewees responded to manuscript validation member-checking).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative thematic study with no quantitative causal effect estimation; donor/IFI financing and national institutional differences are discussed narratively as contextual influences).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative institutional inquiry: Table 3 maps national regulatory structures, constitutional backing, service standards, and legal status of manual pit emptying across Kenya, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia citing primary regulatory ordinances/guidelines [59–63], supplemented by qualitative accounts of conflicting local municipal bylaws and de facto amnesties, though local bylaws are not doctrinally catalogued.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: findings rely on self-reported accounts from senior regulatory managers interviewed remotely in English, with explicit risk of social desirability bias (informants had often gained international recognition for sector reform) and no independent field observation or triangulation with informal sanitation workers or municipal enforcement officers.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / not directly measured: sanitation service scaling, safe emptying practices and voluntary compliance are captured solely through senior regulators' qualitative perceptions rather than empirical measurements of safe faecal sludge containment, transport, disposal or public health outcomes.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: Section 2.6 states that only consensus themes raised consistently across multiple locations were included in Results (potentially under-reporting divergent or negative cases), and illustrative quotes lack anonymized participant codes (e.g., P1–P19) to verify spread across informants, partially mitigated by open deposition of anonymized transcripts in the Cranfield CERES repository.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern for broader transferability: purposive 'positive outliers within positive outliers' sampling targeted 19 senior leaders in 5 reform-leading countries (with snowball referrals, zero local regulator interviews in Mozambique, no reported non-response rate and no inclusion of informal pit emptiers, households or municipal health/environment regulators).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Clear statement of the aims of the research
domain_ratings.justification: The paper explicitly states two clear research aims at the end of the Introduction: understanding how leading national and local regulators work differently to facilitate safe faecal sludge emptying and transport at scale, and assessing whether these practices are transferable across East and Southern Africa.

A qualitative methodology is appropriate because the research investigates how senior national and local regulators interpret implied mandates, navigate legal grey zones, exercise moral courage and build trust with informal pit emptiers.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 (Section 2.2, Overview); PDF Pages 5–6 (Section 2.5, Key informant interviews)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The multi-stage design—synthesizing regulatory literature (26 documents) and secondary qualitative transcripts/Delphi responses (n=37) to build an initial coding framework (Table 1), followed by 19 semi-structured interviews across five purposively selected multi-layered regulatory country cases—is explicitly justified and well aligned with identifying emergent regulatory practices.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Country cases (Kenya, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia) were selected using four explicit purposive criteria targeting 'information rich' positive outliers, and senior managers instrumental to sanitation reform were recruited via partner case studies and snowball referrals. Although invitation refusal counts are not reported and no local regulator was interviewed in Mozambique (Table 2), the positive-outlier recruitment logic is transparent and fit for purpose.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5–6 (Section 2.5, Key informant interviews; Table 2); PDF Page 13 (Section 4.4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection methods are clearly documented: 19 remote semi-structured interviews in English via video conferencing lasting 45–60 minutes between August and December 2024, guided by probing questions informed by prior secondary data, audio/video recorded, transcribed verbatim, and accompanied by a Supplementary interview guide. Trade-offs of remote interviewing are explicitly acknowledged.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly examine their positionality—noting that all authors were trained and employed in Western-headquartered organizations, that 'moral courage' carries European conceptual roots, and that regulated market-based sanitation reflects IFI/Western paradigms—while also noting remote-interview contextual limits and social desirability bias among internationally recognized informants.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 6 (Section 2.5); PDF Page 13 (Section 4.4, Limitations and generalizability)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Ethical approval was granted by Cranfield University Research Ethics System (CURES/23444/2024); advance information sheets and written/verbal informed consent were obtained; anonymized transcripts were returned to participants for validation; and the authors transparently restricted partner secondary transcripts (which lacked formal ethics review) to informing interview design rather than primary reporting.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 (Section 2.1, Ethics); PDF Page 5 (Section 2.4); PDF Page 6 (Section 2.5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While hybrid deductive/inductive thematic analysis in NVivo v14 (Table 1 framework), respondent validation (>70% response) and open transcript archiving (CERES repository) are strengths, Author Contributions list a single analyst ('Formal analysis: Claire Grisaffi') with no mention of double-coding or inter-coder checks, Results excluded non-consensus themes across locations, and quotes carry only generic role labels ('Local regulator'/'National Regulator') without anonymized participant IDs to demonstrate breadth across the 19 interviewees.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 6–7 (Section 2.6, Analysis); PDF Pages 8–10 (Section 3, Results); PDF Page 14 (Author contributions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized around de facto local regulation, barriers to established good practice, moral courage and informal-sector engagement, directly answering both research questions, supported by >70% informant testimonial validation and balanced discussion of counter-perspectives (e.g., national vs local regulator views on financial risk) and study limitations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 7–10 (Section 3, Results); PDF Pages 10–14 (Sections 4 and 5)

domain_ratings.justification: Narrative assessment: The study offers substantial conceptual and policy value for urban sanitation governance in low- and middle-income countries by identifying utilities and municipalities as de facto local regulators and documenting pragmatic, practice-oriented engagement (including tacit amnesties) with informal pit emptiers, enhanced by open-access transcript sharing; value for direct causal inference is bounded by reliance on executive self-report without perspective triangulation from informal workers or households.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable conceptual and policy contribution (with transferability bounded by positive-outlier executive sample and lack of service-provider/household triangulation)
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2 (Data availability statement); PDF Pages 10–14 (Sections 4 and 5)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: S535 is a primary qualitative multi-country study examining how national and local regulators govern urban road-transported faecal sludge emptying and transport in five East and Southern African countries (Kenya, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study demonstrates low-to-moderate methodological concern overall (8 'Yes' items, 1 'Can't tell' item on Q8 data analysis rigor, and strong conceptual value on Q10). Strengths include clear research aims, transparent purposive selection of 'positive outlier' regulatory systems, deductive-inductive coding grounded in literature and secondary qualitative data, formal ethics approval (CURES/23444/2024), respondent validation (>70% informant confirmation), open archiving of anonymized transcripts, and candid reflexivity regarding Western institutional positionality and social desirability bias. Key limitations include single-author formal coding without reported double-coding, filtering of Results to consensus themes across sites, absence of participant IDs on quotes (with zero local regulator interviews in Mozambique), and reliance on senior regulator self-reports without triangulation from informal manual emptiers, competing municipal enforcement agencies or household sanitation outcomes.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 Can't tell item: Q8 data analysis rigor; 0 No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative key-informant interview study (19 semi-structured interviews across 5 purposively selected country cases, informed by literature review and secondary qualitative data synthesis)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methods and ethics: PDF Pages 3–7 (Sections 2.1–2.6, Tables 1–2); Legal/institutional mapping and qualitative results: PDF Pages 7–10 (Sections 3.1–3.5, Table 3); Discussion, reflexivity and limitations: PDF Pages 10–13 (Sections 4.1–4.4); Data availability and author contributions: PDF Pages 2 and 14.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: S535 collects and thematically analyzes primary qualitative semi-structured interviews with 19 senior leaders in national and local regulators (informed by a narrative literature synthesis and qualitative secondary data coding), with no quantitative empirical component or systematic review synthesis; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching appraisal tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
